subject: Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations

messages.author: ca76903a63dd0886
messages.subject: Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
parts:
Hi

I have a question on divergent transitions. I fit a complex nonlinear model, and get an eyewatering number of divergent transitions (3000 divergent transitions when I run three chains of 1500 warmup and 1500 sampling).

Despite this, the Rhat statistic is great (all parameters 1.02 or less), and the mcse / posterior sd are all around 0.03-0.05. The n_eff/n  aren't great though, hovering between 6% and 20% for all parameters, so there is some autocorrelation. My traceplots are little oscillatory, and occasionally sticky, but it doesn't appear to be major.

A posterior predictive check reveals no major problems. My data are very noisy, but as a sanity check, if I were to fit the parameters 'by eye' I would choose similar values to those outputted from the model.

Something tells me that despite this, something is wrong if there are this many divergent transitions. Should I be worried? I've tried to understand the complexities of HMC but I'm very much an applied researcher and not a great physicist, so I don't understand how these divergent transitions influence the samples.

I've read this great summary:
http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html
but it's difficult to test sensitivity to adapt_delta when the models take 5 hours to run each time, even with a small subset of the dataset. I've tried a couple of different values for the subset, but it's not really feasible to try all of this for the large dataset.

My next step is to try the 'non-centered parameterization', but I'm a little unclear exactly how to do the rescaling. Is there a good summary of that somewhere? I've attached my model, in case someone has time for specific tips. (please don't laugh at the likelihood, I know it's a tricky one)

Thanks everyone

Update:
I tried the non-centered parameterization of the type:
in the transformed parameters block:

  matrix[J,K] beta;
  vector[M] alpha;
  for (j in 1:J)
    for (k in 1:K)
      beta[j,k] = sigma_beta[k] * beta_tilde[j,k];
  for (m in 1:M)
    alpha[m] = sigma_alpha * alpha_tilde[m];

in the model block:

for (j in 1:J)
    beta_tilde[j] ~ normal(0, 1); 
  for (m in 1:M)
    alpha_tilde[m] ~ normal(0, 1);

but with no change to the divergences or the inferences. Hope that helps with any suggestions!

Thanks a lot.

messages.author: 2ea7cc7dc67ceaae
messages.subject: Re: Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
parts:
I'm in a similar situation. I have a multilevel nonlinear model that works fine (let'’s call it model 1). After rescaling a parameter from param to 1/param (model 2) the model fit improved (the predicted values are clearly closer to the observed values) but the diverging errors went from 0-5 in model 1 to ~ 5000 in model 2. Diagnostics for model 1 are good and for model 2 similar to what Andy described (everything ok but too many diverging errors). In my case, 'adapt_delta' has no effect on the number of diverging errors - I tried .8, .9, and .99. Hope someone can point us in some directions to understand the reason of those diverging errors. I remember Michael Betancourt at StanCon saying that those errors should not be ignored.

Luca

How did you express the prior on param? The model
probably changed unless you used a Jacobian with a
prior on 1/param that was equivalent to the original
prior on param

- Bob

messages.author: 2ea7cc7dc67ceaae
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
parts:
How did you express the prior on param?  The model
probably changed unless you used a Jacobian with a
prior on 1/param that was equivalent to the original
prior on param

Thank you, Bob. 'param' (called 'rat' in the code below) is the outcome of an equation and has hyperparameters, which I did not change. Some parts of the code:

  rat = rows_dot_product(rat_u, rate[subj]);  # rat_u is a matrix of predictors
  ....
  for (n in 1:N) {
    mu[n] = fmax(0, ast[n] * (1.0 - exp( -rat[n] * (time[n] - itt[n] ) )) );
  }
  ....
  for (i in 1:n_cond_rat_u) {
    rate[,i] ~ normal(mu_r[i], sigma_r[i]);
    sigma_r[i] ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    mu_r[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
  }

In the second version of the model (the one with many diverging errors) I'm using 1/rat:
    mu[n] = fmax(0, ast[n] * (1.0 - exp( -1/rat[n] * (time[n] - itt[n] ) )) );

sigma_r looks better in the second model (less skewed) but as mentioned the number of diverging errors exploded. I was surprised to see meaningful results with so many diverging errors. The second model seems to fit the data better, but there is clearly something that needs to be changed if there are so many diverging errors.

Thank you for the link, next thing I’ll try to recode the model using non-centered parameterization as suggested in the case study.
Thank you for your suggestions and any other suggestion you may have.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
parts:
If all you did is replaced rat[n] with 1/rat[n], then that
does indeed dramatically change the prior on that factor.

In terms of measuring what looks better, I'd suggest simulating
data from known parameters and seeing how well they can be recovered.

- Bob
